How close that \(x\) is to the mean
Where it falls in the spread of the distribution
How similar this participant is to the rest of the sample
How different this participant is from the majority of the sample

title: Z-Scores and Probability Under the Normal Curve
text:
Z-scores
Going backwards: Imagine that \(\color{orange}{s} = 2\) and \(\color{blue}{\bar{x}} = 25\)






Formula


\[x = \color{blue}{\bar{x}} + z\,\color{orange}{s}\]




\(z = 1 \Rightarrow x = 25 + (1)(2) = 27\)
\(z = -2 \Rightarrow x = 25 + (-2)(2) = 21\)
\(z = 0.5 \Rightarrow x = 25 + (0.5)(2) = 26\)

title: Z-Scores and Probability Under the Normal Curve
text:
Calculating a Z-score
Step-by-Step






Two steps



Mean-center the \(x\) values: \(x - \color{blue}{\bar{x}}\) — this makes the mean \(= 0\).
Divide by the standard deviation: \(\dfrac{x - \color{blue}{\bar{x}}}{\color{orange}{s}}\) — this makes the SD \(= 1\).

The average grade on the exam was an 86 with a standard deviation of 4.

title: Z-Scores and Probability Under the Normal Curve
text:
Calculating Probability
What is the probability of scoring a 94 or higher?

The average grade on the exam was an 86 with a standard deviation of 4.

title: Z-Scores and Probability Under the Normal Curve
text:
Calculating Probability
What is the probability of scoring a 94 or higher?






Solution



\(z = \dfrac{x-\color{blue}{\bar{x}}}{\color{orange}{s}} = \dfrac{94-86}{4} = \dfrac{8}{4} = 2\)
Beyond \(z = 2\) is the 2.1% + 0.1% slivers of the curve ≈ 2.3% chance.

Between \(z = -1\) and \(z = 1\): a 68.3% chance of scoring between 82 and 90.

Sample Mean Calculation

A psychology researcher collects the following data on the number of hours five participants spent practicing a task: 3, 5, 8, 2, 7.

Question: What is the average number of hours spent practicing?

SolutionIn R



\(\bar{x} = \frac{\sum(3+5+8+2+7)}{5} = \frac{25}{5} = 5\text{ hours}\)




mean(c(3,5,8,2,7))

[1] 5

2. Mean Calculation
Sample Mean Calculation

A study measures the changes in mood scores before and after an intervention. The changes in mood scores are: -4, -2, 0, 3, 5.

Question: Calculate the mean change in mood score.

SolutionIn R



\(\bar{x} = \frac{\sum(-4 + (-2) + 0 + 3 + 5)}{5} = \frac{2}{5} = 0.4\)




mean(c(-4,-2,0,3,5))

[1] 0.4

title: Exam 1 Review
text:
3. Standard Deviation Calculation
Sample Standard Deviation

A psychologist measures the number of stressful events experienced by a small group of participants over a week: 2, 3, 6, 4, 5.

Question: Calculate the standard deviation of stressful events.

SolutionIn R



Mean: \(\bar{x} = \frac{2+3+6+4+5}{5} = 4\)
Sum of squares: \((2-4)^2+(3-4)^2+(6-4)^2+(4-4)^2+(5-4)^2 = 4+1+4+0+1 = 10\)
\(s = \sqrt{\frac{10}{5-1}} = \sqrt{2.5} \approx 1.58\)




sd(c(2,3,6,4,5))

[1] 1.581139

title: Exam 1 Review
text:
4. Standard Deviation Calculation
Sample Standard Deviation

Sample Standard Deviation Participants’ anxiety scores in a clinical trial are recorded as: 4, 7, 3, 5, 8, 6, 2.

Question: Compute the standard deviation of these anxiety scores.

SolutionIn R



Mean: \(\bar{x} = \frac{4+7+3+5+8+6+2}{7} = \frac{35}{7} = 5\)
Sum of squares: \(1+4+4+0+9+1+9 = 28\)
\(s = \sqrt{\frac{28}{7-1}} = \sqrt{4.67} \approx 2.16\)




sd(c(4,7,3,5,8,6,2))

[1] 2.160247

title: Exam 1 Review
text:
6. Z-Score Calculation
Z-Score for a Single Value

In a personality study, the average score on an extraversion scale is 50, with a standard deviation of 10. One participant scores 70.

Question: What is the Z-score for this participant?

SolutionIn R



\(z = \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma} = \frac{70 - 50}{10} = \frac{20}{10} = 2\)




(70-50)/10

[1] 2

title: Exam 1 Review
text:
7. Z-Score Calculation:
Interpreting Z-Scores

A participant in a self-esteem survey has a Z-score of -1.5. The mean self-esteem score for the survey is 40, and the standard deviation is 5.

Question: Did this participant score above or below the mean, and by how many standard deviations?


Solution


A Z-score of -1.5 is below the mean. In raw score terms: \(X = \mu + z\sigma = 40 + (-1.5)(5) = 40 - 7.5 = 32.5.\) So the participant scored 32.5, which is 1.5 standard deviations below the mean.

title: Exam 1 Review
text:
8. Z-Score Calculation
Z-Score with Negative Value

The mean stress score of a group is 25, with a standard deviation of 4. If a participant has a stress score of 18…

Question: Calculate their Z-score and interpret its meaning in the context of stress levels.

SolutionIn R



\(z = \frac{18 - 25}{4} = \frac{-7}{4} = -1.75.\) The Z-score is \(z \approx -1.75\), meaning this participant’s stress score is 1.75 standard deviations below the group mean — they have substantially lower stress than average.




(18-25)/4

[1] -1.75

title: Exam 1 Review
text:
9. Z-Score Calculation
Multiple Z-Scores

In a clinical assessment, the average depression score is 60, with a standard deviation of 8. Two participants have scores of 72 and 48.

Question: Calculate the Z-scores for both participants and explain what the values tell us about their relative positions in the group.

SolutionIn R



Participant 1 (72): \(z_1 = \frac{72 - 60}{8} = 1.5\). Participant 2 (48): \(z_2 = \frac{48 - 60}{8} = -1.5\).
The first is 1.5 SD above the mean (higher depression than average), the second 1.5 SD below (lower). They are symmetric around the mean.




(72-60)/8;(48-60)/8

[1] 1.5


[1] -1.5

title: Exam 1 Review
text:
10. Z-Scores to Raw Scores
Working Backwards

The distribution of scores on a math test is approximately normal with mean \(\mu = 100\) and standard deviation \(\sigma = 15\).

Question: What raw score corresponds to \(z = 1.2\)?

SolutionIn R



Solve \(z = \frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\) for \(x\): \(x = \mu + z\sigma = 100 + 1.2(15) = 118\)




1.2*15 + 100

[1] 118

What can we do with sample means?

title: Sampling Theory
text:
The Test
Fisher’s rule

Reject \(H_0\) only if she gets all 8 correct.
Under \(H_0\) there are \({8 \choose 4} = \dfrac{8!}{4!\,(8-4)!} = 70\) equally likely ways to guess which 4 cups are milk-first.
So the probability of guessing all 8 correctly by chance is \(\dfrac{1}{70} \approx 1.4\%\).

Since \(1.4\%\) is less than \(5\%\), it is rare enough to count as evidence against \(H_0\).

If she were just guessing, a result this extreme happens about 1.4% of the time. That is evidence she can tell the difference.










6 of 8 correct: fail to reject \(H_0\)


If she were just guessing, getting 6 or more right happens about \(\frac{1 + 16}{70} = 24.3\%\) of the time. That is not unusual enough.





We never prove the alternative; we only judge whether the data are too unlikely under the null.

title: One-Sample T-Test

Why Not z?
From z to t

In lecture 8 we computed \(z = \dfrac{\bar{x} - \mu}{\sigma / \sqrt{n}}\), which needs the population standard deviation \(\sigma\).
In practice we almost never know \(\sigma\), so we substitute the sample’s \(s\).
But \(s\) changes from sample to sample, especially when \(n\) is small. That is extra uncertainty the normal curve does not account for.
So the sampling distribution has heavier tails than the normal curve: the t-distribution. A result must be more extreme to count as unusual.

Introduction to Paired-Samples t-Test
What is a paired-samples t-test?


Paired-Samples t-Test

A statistical method for comparing the means of two related sets of scores, such as the same people measured twice.

title: Paired-Samples T-Test
text:
Purpose of Paired-Samples t-Test
Why use it?

To determine whether there is a statistically significant difference between two related group means.
Useful in psychology for assessing change due to an intervention, therapy, or experiment.

title: Paired-Samples T-Test
text:
Connection to the One-Sample t-Test



A paired-samples t-test is a one-sample t-test on the difference scores.











One-sample


\(t = \dfrac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s / \sqrt{n}}\)
Is the sample mean different from a known value?










Paired


\(t = \dfrac{\bar{D} - 0}{s_D / \sqrt{n}}\)
Is the mean difference \(\bar{D}\) different from 0?

title: Paired-Samples T-Test
text:
Formula for Paired-Samples t-Test
Mathematical representation






Paired-Samples t-Test


\(\large{t = \dfrac{\color{blue}{\bar{D}}}{\color{orange}{s_D}/\sqrt{n}}}\)




\(\color{blue}{\bar{D}}\): mean of the differences between paired observations.
\(\color{orange}{s_D}\): standard deviation of the differences.
\(n\): number of pairs.
Degrees of freedom: \(df = n - 1\).

title: Paired-Samples T-Test
text:
Theoretical Formula Explanation
Understanding each component



Mean difference \(\bar{D}\)

The average of the differences between paired scores.





SD of differences \(s_D\)

How much individual differences vary around the mean difference.





Number of pairs \(n\)

A larger \(n\) shrinks the standard error \(s_D/\sqrt{n}\), so smaller differences can reach significance.

Sampling theory lets us test two unrelated groups.
Under \(H_0\) the difference between group means is centered on 0. Under \(H_A\) it is centered somewhere else.

Inferential Statistics
Applied to independent groups

Our goal is still to test whether a difference is likely due to chance.
With independent samples, chance variation now includes differences between individuals in both groups.

title: Independent-Samples T-Test
text:
Group Variance
Within and between


To compare the means we need to know:

Between-group variance: how much the answers from the experimental group differ from the control group.
Within-group variance: how much the answers of all participants differ from one another.

title: Independent-Samples T-Test
text:
Independent-Samples t-Test Overview
Used when we compare two different groups on a continuous outcome.


local_cafe

smartphone

title: Independent-Samples T-Test
text:
Independent-Samples t-Test
Example

The experimental group drinks caffeinated coffee. The control group drinks decaf. I ask both groups to complete a survey to measure their happiness on a scale of 1 to 10.


The experimental group has a mean happiness score of 8.
The control group has a mean happiness score of 6.


Is the group that drank coffee significantly happier than the control group?

Assumptions

Observations are independent, and the data are randomly sampled. Each person appears in only one group.
Normality: each group’s distribution is approximately normal (or the groups are large enough for the CLT).
Homogeneity of variance: variances are similar across groups (tested with Levene’s Test).

title: Independent-Samples T-Test
text:
Summary: Independent-Samples t-Test

Compares two independent groups.
Tests whether the difference in means is significant.
Uses pooled variance as the denominator when variances are equal (Welch when they are not).
Check assumptions: independence, normality, equal variance (Levene’s Test).
Report the test, the means and SDs, the confidence interval, and an effect size (\(d\)).

title: Independent-Samples T-Test
text:
Computational Formula
Estimating from the samples (pooled t-test)
\[t = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{\sqrt{\color{darkblue}{s_p^2}\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}} \qquad s_p^2 = \frac{(n_1 - 1)s_1^2 + (n_2 - 1)s_2^2}{n_1 + n_2 - 2}\]

\(s_p^2\) = pooled variance, a weighted average of the two group variances.
\(df = n_1 + n_2 - 2\)

title: Independent-Samples T-Test
text:
Computational Formula
When the variances are not equal (Welch’s t-test)
\[t = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{\sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}}\]

No pooling: each group’s variance keeps its own weight, and df is adjusted (it is usually not a whole number).
This is what t.test() does by default in R. Adding var.equal = TRUE gives the pooled version above.

title: Analysis of Variance
text:
Why Not Do More T-Tests?
The problem

Each test is done independently.
None accounts for the shared variability across all groups.
By running multiple t-tests, we increase the probability of a false positive (Type I error) and ignore the combined structure of the data.
ANOVA solves both problems by analyzing all groups at once, partitioning total variance into between-group variance (differences due to the treatment) and within-group variance (random variation).

Alpha inflation

Each test has a 5% chance of a false positive, and those chances accumulate.







Familywise error rate


\(\alpha_\text{FWE} = 1 - (1 - \alpha)^k\)
For three tests: \(1 - (0.95)^3 = 0.1426 \approx 14\%\)

Imagine a group of 5 students is submitting a project, and the total score for the group must be 100 points combined.

That’s n − 1 = 4 degrees of freedom.

Interpreting F
\(MS_B\) is made up of \(MS_E\) + the theoretical difference between groups:

\(MS_B = \text{group difference} + MS_E\)

When \(F < 1\), it’s not likely to be significant.

More than 1 independent variable

Up to now, we’ve looked at experiments that test one question at a time.









t-test


Do two groups differ?
“Does drinking coffee make people happier than not drinking coffee?”










One-way ANOVA

“Does coffee and watching TV make people happier?”

Degrees of freedom



Between groups 1: \(df_{B_1} = k_1 - 1\)
Between groups 2: \(df_{B_2} = k_2 - 1\)

Each MS is an SS divided by its df

Every F uses the same denominator


\(F_A = \dfrac{MS_{B_1}}{MS_{Error}} \qquad F_B = \dfrac{MS_{B_2}}{MS_{Error}} \qquad F_{AB} = \dfrac{MS_{Interaction}}{MS_{Error}}\)

Within-Subjects ANOVA
The key idea






Removing the person


\(SS_{W} = SS_{Subjects} + SS_{Error}\)
\(SS_{Error} = SS_{W} - SS_{Subjects}\)




In between-subjects ANOVA, differences between people sit inside the error term.
In within-subjects ANOVA we subtract them out, so the error is smaller and the test is more powerful.

title: Within-Subjects ANOVA
text:
Calculating Repeated-Measures ANOVA






The F ratio


\(F = \dfrac{MS_{Time}}{MS_{Error}}\)
\(MS_{Time} = \dfrac{SS_{Time}}{df_{Time}} = \dfrac{SS_{Time}}{k - 1}\)
\(MS_{Error} = \dfrac{SS_{W} - SS_{Subjects}}{df_{Error}} = \dfrac{SS_{W} - SS_{Subjects}}{(n-1)(k-1)}\)




\(k\) is the number of time points (or conditions) and \(n\) is the number of participants.

text:
Degrees of Freedom






Rules



Time: \(df_{Time} = k - 1\)
Subjects: \(df_{Subjects} = n - 1\)
Error: \(df_{Error} = (n - 1) \times (k - 1)\)

title: Within-Subjects ANOVA
text:
Interpreting F






What F means


\(MS_{Time}\) is made up of \(MS_{Error}\) + the theoretical change over time:

\(MS_{Time} = \text{change over time} + MS_{Error}\)
If there is no change: \(MS_{Time} = 0 + MS_{Error}\), so \(F = \dfrac{MS_{Error}}{MS_{Error}} = 1\).
If there is a change: \(F = 1 + \dfrac{\text{change}}{MS_{Error}}\), which is greater than 1.





When \(F \leq 1\), it’s not likely to be significant.

title: Within-Subjects ANOVA
text:
Hypothesis Testing: ANOVA






Decision rule



\(F \leq 1\): fail to reject the null hypothesis.
\(F > 1\): compare to the critical value (or use the p-value). Reject \(H_0\) only if \(p < \alpha\).

Regression is the multivariate version of correlation.

Regression terminology
Outcome and predictors



\(Y\)

The outcome variable: the one we choose to predict.





\(\hat{Y}\)

The predicted value of \(Y\) from the model.





\(A\), \(B\), etc.

The predictor variables we have reason to believe predict \(Y\) (one or more).

Regression terminology


Regress

Regression Equation
Step-by-step
\[
\large{\color{red}{Y_i} = \color{green}{\beta_0} + \color{blue}{\beta_1(A)}+\color{orange}{e_i}}
\]

1. The observed value of \(Y\) for a particular participant (\(i\))


2. Intercept: the predicted \(Y\) when all predictors are 0


3. Coefficient (weight): the predicted change in \(Y\) for a one-unit increase in \(A\)


4. The value of a particular participant on the measure of \(A\)


5. Error: random, and therefore cannot be predicted

title: Linear Regression
text:
Linear Regression
Least squares

The line of best fit is the line that makes the residuals as small as possible.
A residual is the distance between an observed \(Y\) and its predicted \(\hat{Y}\): \(e_i = Y_i - \hat{Y}_i\).
Least squares picks the line that minimizes the sum of the squared residuals, \(\sum e_i^2\).

title: Linear Regression
text:
Regression
Equation component meanings

\(Y\) = the actual, observed \(y\) value for a participant
\(\hat{Y}\) = the model’s predicted \(y\) value for a participant
\(\beta_0\) = the intercept: the predicted \(y\) when \(A\) is 0
\(A\) = the \(A\) value for a participant
\(\beta_1\) = the coefficient for \(A\): it is multiplied by \(A\) and added to \(\beta_0\) to estimate \(y\)

More than one X






Multiple regression


\(\large{\hat{Y}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1(A) + \beta_2(B) + \cdots}\)

\(\beta_1\) and \(\beta_2\) are the coefficients for predictors \(A\) and \(B\).
Each coefficient is the predicted change in \(Y\) for a one-unit increase in that predictor, holding the other predictors constant.

How much can we account for?

\(R^2\) is the correlation coefficient (\(r\)) squared, and is always between 0 and 1.
In correlation, it is the amount of \(y\) accounted for by \(x\).
In regression, \(R^2\) is the amount of \(y\) accounted for by all of the predictors together.
Did we account for a significant amount of the variance in \(y\)?

Linearity: the relationship between each predictor and \(y\) is linear.
Independence: the observations (and residuals) are independent.
Homoscedasticity: the residuals have about the same spread at every predicted value.
Normality: the residuals are approximately normal.
No severe multicollinearity: the predictors are not nearly duplicates of one another.

title: Linear Regression
text:
Assumptions of Linear Regression






Assumptions



Linearity: the relationship between each predictor and \(y\) is linear.
Independence: the observations (and residuals) are independent.
Homoscedasticity: the residuals have about the same spread at every predicted value.
Normality: the residuals are approximately normal.
No severe multicollinearity: the predictors are not nearly duplicates of one another.

Standard deviation: how different are participants from the average?
Height: \(M = 5'6"\), \(s = 2\) inches










Bivariate


Covariance: do the variables vary in the same way?
Does the spread-out-ness of height overlap with the spread-out-ness of weight?

title: Covariance & Correlation
text:
Covariance

Professor Brocker wants to know if how many cups of coffee a professor drinks daily impacts their happiness. He asks 50 professors how many cups they have in a typical day and then has them rate their happiness on a scale of 1 to 10.


Variable 1: number of cups of coffee (continuous)
Variable 2: happiness (continuous)

title: Covariance & Correlation
text:
Covariance
Two things we could find

The variance of each variable on its own.
The covariance of the two variables together.



Covariance refers to how two continuous variables vary in tandem.

Generally, if cups of coffee goes up, what does happiness tend to do?
Generally, if happiness goes up, what does cups of coffee tend to do?

title: Covariance & Correlation
text:
Covariance
The formula






Covariance


\(COV_{XY} = \dfrac{\Sigma(X-\bar{X})(Y-\bar{Y})}{N-1}\)









Well, well, well… we meet again


\(s^2 = \dfrac{\Sigma(X-\bar{X})^2}{N-1} = \dfrac{\Sigma(X-\bar{X})(X-\bar{X})}{N-1}\)




The variance of a variable is the covariance of that variable with itself.

title: Covariance & Correlation
text:
Covariance
Let’s break it down






Steps



Find the mean of each variable: \(\bar{X} = \dfrac{\Sigma X}{n}\) and \(\bar{Y} = \dfrac{\Sigma Y}{n}\).
Subtract the mean of \(X\) from each \(X\) value, and the mean of \(Y\) from each \(Y\) value: \((X-\bar{X})\) and \((Y-\bar{Y})\).
Multiply the deviation scores of \(X\) with the deviation scores of \(Y\): \((X-\bar{X})(Y-\bar{Y})\).
Sum the products: \(\Sigma(X-\bar{X})(Y-\bar{Y})\).
Divide by \(N-1\): \(\dfrac{\Sigma(X-\bar{X})(Y-\bar{Y})}{N-1}\).

text:

In R

covariance.R

cov(ex$Cups, ex$Happiness)   # covariance

[1] 3.2

var(ex$Cups)                 # the variance is a covariance with itself

[1] 3.2

cov(ex$Cups, ex$Cups)        # same number

[1] 3.2

title: Covariance & Correlation
text:
Covariance
What does it tell us?
Covariance is the bivariate equivalent of variance.

The sign tells us the direction: positive means the variables tend to rise together.
But the size is hard to interpret. It is in odd units (cups × happiness points) and changes if we change the scale.
Variance had the same problem (squared units), so we took the square root to get the standard deviation. For covariance, we standardize it.

title: Covariance & Correlation
text:
Correlation
Standardized covariance






Pearson correlation


\(r = \dfrac{cov_{xy}}{(SD_x)(SD_y)} = \dfrac{\Sigma(X-\bar{X})(Y-\bar{Y})}{(SD_x)(SD_y)(N-1)}\)




Correlation is the standardized covariance: we divide the covariance by the standard deviation of \(x\) times the standard deviation of \(y\).
Just as a z-score puts a score on a unit-free scale, \(r\) puts the relationship on a unit-free scale.

title: Covariance & Correlation
text:
Correlation
Back to the worked example






Compute r


\(r = \dfrac{cov_{xy}}{(SD_x)(SD_y)} = \dfrac{3.20}{(1.79)(1.86)} = 0.96\)




correlation.R

cor(ex$Cups, ex$Happiness)

[1] 0.9607689




A strong positive correlation: professors who drink more coffee tend to report higher happiness.

title: Covariance & Correlation
text:
Correlation
Bounded between -1 and +1










Closer to -1 is a negative correlation, closer to +1 is a positive correlation, and closer to 0 means no correlation.

title: Covariance & Correlation
text:
Correlation
The Pearson Product-Moment Correlation (Pearson, 1895)

The sign indicates the direction.
The number indicates the magnitude (strength) of the relationship:







Rules of thumb



0.1 is a small correlation
0.3 is a moderate correlation
0.5 or higher is a large correlation

title: Covariance & Correlation
text:
Correlation and \(R^2\)

Correlation is written \(r\).
If we square \(r\), we get \(R^2\), which is always positive.
\(R^2\) is the proportion of variance the two variables share:

the amount of \(y\) accounted for by \(x\),
and the amount of \(x\) accounted for by \(y\).

title: Covariance & Correlation
text:
Correlation and \(R^2\)
Example

Students’ grades in MTH 110 and their grades in this course correlate at \(r = 0.3\).


A moderate correlation.
How much of your grade in this course is accounted for by your MTH 110 grade?







Compute \(R^2\)


\(R^2 = r^2 = 0.3 \times 0.3 = 0.09\), so 9% of the variance in your grade is accounted for by your MTH 110 grade.

title: Covariance & Correlation
text:
Is the Correlation Significant?
Testing \(H_0: \rho = 0\)

Our sample \(r\) estimates the population correlation \(\rho\). Is it different from 0?







The test


\(t = \dfrac{r\sqrt{n-2}}{\sqrt{1-r^2}} \qquad df = n - 2\)




Example: \(r = 0.35\) with \(n = 50\) gives \(t(48) = 2.59\), \(p\) = .013: a significant (moderate) positive correlation.

Pitfalls
What can go wrong with \(r\)?












\(r\) measures linear relationships only, is pulled around by outliers, and shrinks when the range of one variable is restricted. Always plot your data.

title: Covariance & Correlation
text:
Interpreting Correlation





We don’t use the words caused or resulting from.
When reporting \(r\): “As x goes up, y tends to go up.”
When reporting \(R^2\): “z% of the variance in y is accounted for by x.”
A third variable could explain both, and the direction could run either way.

title: Covariance & Correlation
text:
Summary: Covariance & Correlation

Covariance is how two variables vary together: the bivariate equivalent of variance.
Correlation (\(r\)) is the standardized covariance: unit-free, bounded between -1 and +1.
The sign gives the direction and the size gives the strength; \(r^2\) is the shared variance.
Test \(H_0: \rho = 0\) with \(t = r\sqrt{n-2}/\sqrt{1-r^2}\), \(df = n - 2\).
Plot your data: outliers, curves and restricted ranges can fool \(r\).
Correlation does not imply causation.

Professor Brocker’s PSY 348 midterm had 40 students. The exam scores were approximately normally distributed with a mean of 76 and a standard deviation of 8.

Nadia’s score is 1.5 standard deviations above the mean

title: Statistical Formulas
text:
Inferential Statistics

Single Sample T-Test
\(t = \frac{\bar{x}-\mu}{\sigma_{\bar{x}}}\)

\(t\) = The t-statistic, representing how far the sample mean is from the population mean (in standard error units).
\(\bar{X}\) = The sample mean of your data.
\(\mu_0\) = The hypothesized population mean (the value you’re comparing your sample to).
\(\sigma_{\bar{X}}\) = The standard error of the mean, calculated as:

\(\sigma_{\bar{X}} = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\)




Paired-Samples T-Test
\(t = \frac{\bar{D}}{\sigma_{\bar{D}}}\)

\(\bar{D}\) = Mean difference between T1 and T2
\(\sigma_{\bar{D}}\) = Standard Error of the mean difference

\(\sigma_{\bar{D}} = \frac{s_D}{\sqrt{n}}\) (where \(s_D\) is the sample SD of the difference scores)




Independent-Samples T-Test
\(t = \frac{\bar{X}_1-\bar{X}_2}{\sqrt{\frac{s^2_1}{N_1}+\frac{s^2_2}{N_2}}}\)

\(t\) = The t-statistic, representing how far apart the two sample means are, relative to the variability in the data.
\(\bar{X}_1\) and \(\bar{X}_2\) = The means of the two independent samples (Group 1 and Group 2).
\(s_1^2\) and \(s_2^2\) = The sample variances of the two groups.
\(n_1\) and \(n_2\) = The sample sizes of the two groups.



One-Way ANOVA (Between)
\(F = \frac{MS_{\text{between}}}{MS_{\text{within}}} = \frac{\frac{SS_{\text{between}}}{df_{\text{between}}}}{\frac{SS_{\text{within}}}{df_{\text{within}}}}\)

\(F\) = Test statistic for the ANOVA
\(MS_{between}\) = Mean Square Between Groups
\(MS_{within}\) = Mean Square Within Groups (also called Error)
\(SS_{between}\) = Sum of Squares Between Groups
\(SS_{within}\) = Sum of Squares Within Groups
\(df_{between}\) = Degrees of Freedom Between Groups
\(df_{within}\) = Degrees of Freedom Within Groups

What is Statistics?
Definition and Terminology

Statistics

The field of describing, analyzing, and making inferences based on data either from a sample or a population

Describing

What does the data ‘look’ like?

Analyzing

A mathematical approach to extracting information about the data

Inferences

Applying logical reasoning to predict what might happen in subsequent measurements. Typically, inferences are made from samples and extrapolated into what the population might be ‘expected’ to look like.

Data

Qualitative or Quantitative information that consists of measured or manipulated variables

Sample

A subset of the population of interest

Population

The entire set of interest.

title: Welcome to Statistics for Psychology!
text:
Data Literacy
Why Do I Need It
Statistical and data literacy is useful for being able to make informed decisions — especially when a claim is designed to grab your attention before you’ve had a chance to think it through.

If you saw a headline claiming that blueberries could cure cancer, wouldn’t it be helpful to know how to evaluate that claim before sharing it?


How many blueberries, and how “cancer” was even measured?
How long do you have to eat them for?
Is it all types of cancer or a specific one?
Is it truly that blueberries cure cancer, or are they mixed in with something else (diet, exercise, a specific compound at a dose no one eats naturally)?


This is the same skill you’ll use on every “coffee causes/cures ___” headline for the rest of your life.

Wouldn’t it be nice if…
We tend to describe the world the way we wish it were, not always the way it actually is. A few examples of that:

Dogs smiled (that “smile” is often a stress signal, not happiness)
Birdsong is always beautiful (some of it is territorial alarm-calling)
All animals love their children (infanticide is documented across many species)

Our brain is a pattern matching machine

We look for information that confirms our thoughts and surroundings
We would (often) prefer that things were nice and pretty, but reality is often not so simple

What is Research?
Research is a systematic process of asking a question about the world and collecting evidence to answer it — as opposed to relying on intuition, anecdote, or “everybody knows that…”


It’s systematic: it follows a planned, repeatable process (not a one-off guess).
It’s testable: it produces a claim that data could, in principle, prove wrong.
It’s shareable: the methods and data are reported clearly enough that someone else could check your work.

title: Scales of Measurement and Measures of Central Tendency
text:
Measures of Central Tendency
Median






Important



The middle number; obtained by ordering all values from lowest to highest and taking the middle (if n is odd or the average of the 2 middle if n is even)
\(\large{x = \{4,2,5,6,3\}}\)
\(\large{x = \{2,3,4,5,6\}}\)
\(\large{x = \{2,3,\color{blue}{4},5,6\}}\)






Why does income get reported as a median instead of a mean?

Income distributions are heavily right-skewed by a small number of very high earners, which pulls the mean upward. The median isn’t affected by those extreme values, so it better represents what a “typical” person actually earns.
For example, O*NET reports the 2025 median annual wage for Psychologists as $110,840 (O*NET OnLine, 19-3039.00) – a handful of very high (or very low) earners in the field wouldn’t shift that median the way they’d shift a mean.



When would you want this for research?

Any time your variable is skewed or outlier-prone – reaction times, wait times, salaries, hospital stays – the median gives a more honest sense of the “typical” case than the mean does.

A skewed distribution occurs when one side of the data gets cut off due to measurement limitation.

What does it do?

You scored an 82. Is that good?


You can’t say yet — good compared to what?
Standard deviation describes how spread out the whole group is — but only in the variable’s own units (exam points, inches, dollars…).
A z-score places one score on a common ruler: how many standard deviations it sits from the mean.
Because that ruler has no units, it can answer “compared to what?” for any measurement.

Why Do We Care?


A z-score tells me where my score falls in SD units.
I can then look at this standard normal curve, and estimate what percentage of people did better or worse than me.

Why Do We Care?

The mean score for Exam 1 was a 92 with a standard deviation of 3.




Esmeralda scored an 86.
What percent of the class scored better than Esmeralda?
\(z=\frac{x-\bar{x}}{s} = \frac{86-92}{3} = -2\)
98% of the class did better than Esmeralda.
